# Psalm 89:27–52: research notes

I found good material for most verses, but some gaps remain. I ran out of searches before I could check verses 40–48 one at a time, so the notes there are thinner. I found nothing for Lutheran, Anglican or Pentecostal teachers on this passage (apart from one Luther mention under v. 37). I also found no Orthodox source, no Bible Odyssey article and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it. All of those are left out.

**Big picture (vv. 27–52)**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says the psalm moves from soaring praise of God's covenant with David into lament over a present crisis that seems to contradict all those promises, and closes with hard-won praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- **When the crisis happened is disputed:**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggest perhaps Absalom's rebellion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_089.cfm
  - The Geneva Study Bible points either to the kingdom splitting under Jeroboam or, as prophecy, to the Babylonian captivity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-39.htm
  - Matthew Henry weighs both Rehoboam's time and Zedekiah's. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-39.html
  - Ellicott thinks the persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes fits best. He also says the "servant" and "anointed" may be the whole nation pictured as one Davidic prince. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/89.htm

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: Jesse's youngest son became the "firstborn," God's favourite son, and the title here covers the whole line of David's kings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/89.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): "firstborn" isn't always literal. It often signifies simply a well-beloved, or best-beloved son. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-27.html
- Pulpit Commentary: there is only one true Firstborn, Christ. Israel, Ephraim and David are reflections of him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-27.htm
- Gill (Baptist) reads the verse of Christ, the firstborn from the dead and King of kings. He notes that Jewish writers also read it of the Messiah. Cambridge Bible: John borrowed from this verse and v. 37 for his title "the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-27.htm
- NET Bible note (modern scholarship): a firstborn son usually had special status and privileges. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=psa&chapter=89&verse=27

**v. 28**
- Pulpit links the verse back to 2 Samuel 7:15–16 and 23:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/89.htm
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: in Jesus the covenant is ratified both by blood of sacrifice and by oath of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-89.cfm

**v. 29**
- Ellicott: "days of heaven" echoes Deuteronomy 11:21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/89.htm
- Guzik: this promise is fulfilled only in the forever reign of Jesus the Messiah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-89.cfm
- Augustine (Catholic, Church Father) contrasts the "days of heaven" with earthly thrones, whose days are almost gone before they have come. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm

**vv. 30–32**
- Pulpit lists the kings who fell away, beginning with Solomon and going on through Rehoboam, Manasseh, Jehoiakim and others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/89.htm
- Ellicott: the poet saw the exile as the punishment foretold here. On that view the sin had been paid for, which is why Israel's continued suffering was so puzzling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/89.htm
- Matthew Henry (Concise): It is a rod which they shall never feel, but when there is need. He also calls it a rod, not a sword: meant to correct, not destroy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-27.htm
- Haydock (Catholic), following Augustine, on this verse (numbered 31 in the Douay): Christ will never lose his Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/psalms-88.html

**vv. 33–34: where Protestant readers differ (believers' security)**
- StudyLight notes that its commentators divide five ways here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-33.html
- **Reformed/Calvinist:**
  - Gill (Baptist) says God's love is never taken from Christ or from anyone "chosen in him." Only the felt sense of that love is sometimes withdrawn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-33.htm
  - Barnes (Presbyterian): God would not suffer him to become wholly apostate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-33.html
  - Geneva Study Bible: even when the faithful fall short, God won't break his covenant with them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-33.htm
- **A more cautious reading:**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: individual kings could be faithless and punished, but the line's role as a type of Christ continues. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_089.cfm
  - The Homiletical Commentary points out that the text says "him" (the family), not "them" (the sinners). It still sees a parallel between Christ and his Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-33.html
- I found no Wesleyan or Arminian treatment of this verse.
- **Language notes:**
  - Cambridge Bible suggests changing one letter to match 1 Chronicles 17:13 ("take away"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-33.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch: God will not "profane" the covenant, meaning loose its sacred bonds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-33.htm

**v. 35**
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): swearing by his holiness, God stakes his own holy character on keeping the promise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-89.cfm
- Keil & Delitzsch read "one thing have I sworn" rather than the Septuagint's "once for all." They note that 2 Samuel 7 has no formal oath, but the poetry treats the promise as one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-33.htm

**v. 36**
- Spurgeon: David's line is endless in Jesus, and continues in each generation of believers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps089.cfm
- Matthew Henry: the meaning differs depending on whether you apply it to David's successors or to Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_089.cfm
- Pulpit (on v. 4): the promise was not fulfilled "in the letter," because no Davidic king reigned after Zerubbabel's time. It was fulfilled in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/89.htm

**v. 37**
- **Who is the "faithful witness in the sky"?**
  - Ellicott says the moon, the "arbiter" of Israel's festivals, which were signs of the covenant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/89.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch note that Luther, Hengstenberg and Jewish expositors each took the line differently. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-33.htm
- Augustine (Catholic): the sun stands for the perfected mind and the moon for the body perfected in the resurrection. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801089.htm

**v. 38**
- Ellicott: the boldness of this complaint has scandalised the Jewish expositors. But the poem loses its point if we soften it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/89.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) reads it as "Thou hast despised us, and delayed the coming of the Messias." He rejects the charge that the psalmist was impatient. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/psalms-88.html
- Seedbed (Methodist): the psalmist feels that God hasn't kept his side of the covenant. https://seedbed.com/the-difficult-journey-of-faith-psalm-89/

**v. 39**
- Guzik: Ethan *knew* God hadn't renounced the covenant, but in the crisis it *felt* as if he had. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-89.cfm
- Pulpit: the verb is very rare, found elsewhere only in Lamentations 2:7. The crown was so holy that any disgrace to it counted as "profanation." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-39.htm
- Matthew Henry: We misconstrue the rebukes of Providence if we think they make void the covenant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-39.html
- Gill reads this of Christ: the crown of thorns and the mocking "if" at the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-39.html

**vv. 40–42**
- Keil & Delitzsch: these verses draw mainly on Psalm 80:13. The "hedges" are the protective boundaries of the king's land. They picture most of the kingdom lost and Egypt threatening the rest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/89-39.htm

**vv. 44–45**
- Matthew Henry: God had not only dethroned the king but put an end to the kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-39.html
- Guzik: the king himself, whether David, Solomon or a later king, was personally weakened by the crisis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Coffman, quoting the Wycliffe commentary, applies "the days of his youth" to the 18-year-old king taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-39.html

**vv. 46–48**
- Guzik:
  - The psalmist may be praying for a weary king, or longing to see the kingdom vindicated before he dies.
  - The question in v. 48 expects the answer "no": no one can save himself from the grave.
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-89.cfm
- Matthew Henry: if there were no life after death, man might seem made in vain. Since God doesn't make man in vain, the psalmist asks him to remember those kindnesses. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_089.cfm
- Haydock (Catholic): Augustine read "remember what my substance is" (v. 47) as pointing to Christ taking on our nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/psalms-88.html

**v. 49**
- Guzik: Ethan refuses to stay with the idea that God has cast them off. He appeals to what God swore to David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-89.cfm
- Homiletical Commentary: the "former lovingkindnesses" were past mercies, taken as pledges of mercies still to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/89-33.html

**vv. 50–51**
- Guzik: Ethan asks God to notice how low and despised his people are, since God's enemies are the king's enemies too. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-89.cfm
- Seedbed (Methodist): "anointed one" is "Messiah" in Hebrew and "Christ" in Greek. https://seedbed.com/the-difficult-journey-of-faith-psalm-89/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compare the plea to Isaiah 37:17–35. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_089.cfm

**v. 52**
- Binnie, quoted by Spurgeon: this closing praise belongs to all of Book Three of the Psalms, ought not to be treated as if it were merely the last verse of Psalm 89. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-89/
- Seedbed: this stubborn hope is the sombre note that ends Book Three. https://seedbed.com/the-difficult-journey-of-faith-psalm-89/
